(p1: beginning frame; p2: another angle of the bundle.)

(a) Meditation on Gaṇeśa; (b) Hymn to Śiva; (c) Meditation on the Bull; (d) Meditation on Bālasubrahmaṇya; (e) The Eight Verses on the Feet of Śiva. (p. 3a) (f.a) This book of words by Kuppusvāmī is a book of verses concerning Śiva. (p. 3b) (f. 1b)
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, and has four arms; he has a serene countenance— for the pacification of all obstacles.
The elephant-faced one, inconceivable, with sharp tusks and three eyes, possessing a vast belly,
the complete form of all beings, the ancient one—
the Lord of the Gods, red in color, who is well-worshipped by the immortals.
I bow to the Lord, the son of Paśupati, the King of Obstacles.

Because he destroyed Kandarpa, because he swallowed the poison, because he humbled the pride of Kāla, because he shattered the three cities that were the abode of the Daityas, and because he triumphed at Dakṣa’s sacrifice; (l. 2)

He is superior even to Pārvatī because he bestows weapons upon the son of Pṛthā, because he grants victory to Nṛsiṃha, because he is the source of prosperity for Mādhava, and because he is the fulfiller of the Teacher’s [Śiva’s] commands;
he is superior to Paśupati because he is the beloved of Gāyatrī and because he was propitiated by the son of Daśaratha.
O Śauri, because you delighted in the account of the journey to Kailāsa by granting his desired progeny,
and because Viṣṇu worshipped you with his own eye along with a thousand lotuses;
and furthermore, O Paśupati, because of the favor of the discus, you are the most excellent among all the gods.
Because they are constantly worshipped by many people on earth, because Viṣṇu— possessing tenfold forms— honored them by bestowing the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*),
and because the feet of Brahmā, the slayer of Mura, and Śeṣa rested upon their bodies while they bore the forms of a swan, a boar, and a man-lion respectively.
Moreover, if Paśupati—who is liberated even from the weapon of giving and is the most excellent among all gods—is the creator of the entire world;
and if Śiva, who possesses the form of Ambā, is [the creator];
and if the entirety of the Purāṇas along with the Āgamas is authoritative; [then so too is this].
O Great-Souled One, if there be any prosperity for one who wears rudrākṣa beads,
may there be no misfortune whatsoever for the enemy;
on his feet let there be anklets and small bells, and let his hips be adorned with a broad girdle.
In his hand [he holds] a trident, a skull-bowl, a ḍakka-drum, and a ḍamaru; around his neck is the Hālāhala poison;
in his ear is a serpent-earring; he has three eyes and blazing fire upon his forehead—thus I bow to Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara, the Lord of Ambikā, who performs the Tāṇḍava dance.
While the sounds of the *nandi*, maddala, and vādyapiñcana instruments resounded,
Brahmā, having struck the rhythmic beat (*tāla*), uttered "kiṭata-tattattattale tāntām" for each respective measure.
Tumburu and Nārada sang "tānanam tānanam tānanam" for Śambhu;
and his dance was performed with the sounds "jhāṃ jhāṃ jhāṃ jhatām.
[The asterisms] Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā belong to the sign of Aries.
The three quarters of Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and half of Mṛgaśiras constitute Taurus. Half of Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, and Punarvasu constitute Gemini.
One quarter of Punarvasu, Puṣya, and the final portion of Āśleṣā constitute Cancer.
The three constellations beginning with Maghā constitute one quarter of Leo;

the three constellations beginning with Uttarā-phalgunī constitute one quarter of Virgo; Hasta and half of Citrā constitute Libra; half of Citrā, Svāti, and the three constellations beginning with Viśākhā constitute Scorpio.
The last quarter of Viśākhā, Anurādhā, and Jyeṣṭhā constitute Scorpio.
Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and one quarter of Uttarāṣāḍhā constitute Sagittarius.
Two quarters of Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, and half of Dhaniṣṭhā constitute Capricorn.
The half of Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and the three [asterisms] beginning with Pūrvābhādrapadā constitute Aquarius;
Pūrvabhādrapadā and those ending with Revatī constitute Pisces.
Pisces and Aries have four quarters each, while Taurus and Aquarius have four eighths each.
Five *kārsāpaṇas* and five *tulās* [should be given] for the purpose of the bow and the crab;
five and four for the scorpion, the capricorn, the lion, and the twins;
eight and four at the raising of the banner; and five and seven at the chariot festival.
Afterwards, there is the eighth purification, the consecration by the jar following the sacrifice,
and the meditation on the Bull.
The four-footed form is that of the Veda, while its horn is the form of Agni;
the sun and moon are its eyes, and Rudra is likewise its mouth.
The six treatises are said to be its tail, and the ritual ordinance is called its hair.
Upon his bull are all the sacred fords (tīrthas), and a garland of jewels upon his chest;
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are at his sides, and he is said to have the form of a bull.
With five faces, equal mouths, and equal crowns and eyes;
with ten ears, ten arms, ten tridents, and ten [attributes];
with one throat and a heart that is intensely red in color.
The nature of the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*) is twelve cubits in measure; such is the form of the sacrificial pedestal. (l2.
[It should be made from] bamboo, *jāti*, *palāśa*, sandalwood trees, *bilva*, as well as *khadira*, *nyagrodha*, *nṛpanāli*, coconut, betel nut, *tāla*, *śamī*, and *campaka*. (l3.)
The Mādhūka, Bakula, mango, and jackfruit trees arose among the gods;
[therein] the Lord of Gods was fashioned together with the bull-bannered one, bearing a staff as his weapon.
(1) One foot, two arms, three eyes, adorned with a line of hair like a cord of darbha grass. (2)
His body is white in form, bearing the appearance of a lotus-seat and a staff-emblem mounted upon his parrot-like nose;
he wears matted locks of red flames, bears the moon, and is composed of red-bodied radiance;
in his hands he holds a trident, a skull-cup, a noose, and a ḍamaru drum—he is the protector of the world.

I praise the auspicious protector of the field, Vaṭuka, the lord of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, who has the form of Nirvāṇa, whose vehicle is a dog, who possesses three eyes, who is a tumultuous roar of bliss,
who is naked, who has the form of a yakṣa, four arms, and holds a snake-noose, a trident, and a skull-cup.
I bow to the one with upward-pointing hair, holding a *ḍamaru* drum and a dog, who embodies the nature of the Field Protector (*kṣetrapāla*).

I worship the Lord born of Rudra, who has the luster of coral, possesses a single face, and holds a vajra, a spear, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands; he is the slayer of the enemies of the world of gods and the bestower of freedom from obstacles. I take refuge in him whose vehicle is the peacock.
O friend, [he is] mounted upon a chariot, possessing the brilliant luster of ten thousand rising suns, with six faces shining forth;
he has twelve eyes and is adorned with ornaments made of jewels.
He holds in his hands a book of knowledge, a spear, a cock, a bow, arrows, a sword, and a shield.
I worship the primordial Mahāsena, who bears the lotus of causes within his heart.
The *asura-haraharāstra*, the trident with its tip encircled by flames,
which brings an end to all the gods, shall be held in the hand of Śambhu;
it possesses three points, contains fire, and has the nature of wind and space.
Having the brilliance of one fallen into fire, with the very form of the deity of the weapon—
this is the meditation on Pradoṣanāyaka.
One whose limbs resemble rubies, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, and possesses three eyes; who holds an axe and a deer, with Gaurī at his left side;
who displays the gesture of fearlessness and wears bracelets on his wrists, adorned with necklaces and armlets.
The meditation on Daṇḍapāṇi: his head is adorned with a garland of the petals of white lotuses, and he is the leader of the Śrībali.

I praise Skanda, the son of Kātyāyanī, who has the radiance of a lotus and the dawn, who possesses two arms and a single mind-born face; he bows to the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*), wears a garment on his left hip, and holds a staff in his right hand.
He bears a *rudrākṣa* rosary, holds fire in his hand, is accompanied by the moon, his limbs are smeared with ashes, and he is radiant upon a lotus seat.
I bow to the one whose vehicle is fire, who is equal to the upward-flowing Gaṅgā, who is the syllable Oṃ, the root mantra accompanied by a host of jewels;
I praise the essence of the Vedas, the one named Śiva, the Lord of Kailāsa, the teacher of all people—the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Having stepped upon the past with one foot and placed another foot multiplied above it, he explains all words for the sages who share in his portion during the great festival at his own abode.

May the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who eternally bears in his lotus-like hands a serpent, the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyānamudrā*), a flame, and a book with his four [hands], hasten before me. (3) This is the meditation on Caṇḍeśvara. (4)
With his right hand holding a chisel that resembles a pair of joined jewels, and with one peaceful face resting upon his left thigh;
his body is smeared with ashes and clothed in white garments, intensely devoted to the sound of meditation upon the feet of Śambhu;
he has two eyes, two arms, is dark-complexioned, and indeed holds a chisel.
And especially the Kaṭaka, as well as the Vyākhyāmudrā and the Meva.
Two-footed, clothed in garments, adorned with all ornaments,
likewise endowed with a crown of matted locks and possessing the form of primordial wisdom—
by the mere clapping of hands, the fruit shall be like that of Śiva.
The *nirmālya* (remnant offering), however, is especially always the form of meditation (*dhyānarūpaka*).
[One should meditate on] the illustrious one with two locks of hair and a crown, a beautiful face, two ears adorned with crocodile-shaped earrings, and a sacred thread;
with palms joined in *añjali*, the victorious right arm holding a chisel, and Caṇḍeśvara together with the lotus-foot of Śiva on the left.
Meditation on Vāgīśa:
I bow to the Lord of Speech, whose head is adorned with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads and engaged in the worship of Śiva; who has a gentle face, auspicious eyes, and ears graced by ornaments;
whose hands are joined in añjali, and whose left side bears the weapons of the three strides; who holds his daughter Vidyā on his lap, and who is the excellent Master of Words.
The Meditation on Vātapurīśa
He has one face, one body, two eyes, and two hands; his [right] hand is in the gesture of salutation (*añjali*) and his [left] hand holds the book in the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*).
He is devoted to the *Drāviḍa-bhāṣya* commentary on the *Pañcākṣara*, which he holds in his left hand during the festival of the full moon.
His beautiful face is adorned with two locks of hair and a crest-jewel; his right and left hands hold the book and the seal known as Knowledge (*jñāna*).
I worship him who wears a garland, has a face like a lotus, bears the sacred thread, and stands with feet firm; he whose speech is of ruby and who is the great object of devotion.
This is the meditation on the connection to knowledge.
The state of childhood is naked in form, surrounded by matted locks; there are two eyes in the pair of leaves.
On the side of the tip of the right hand and on both soles of the feet, there is the dance of the right Knowledge-breast.
On the right, with the needle of the index finger, there is the vessel of the breast on the other side; this is the Śaiva [form].
I bow to Siddhāntaveda, who is endowed with all arts and possesses the awakening of knowledge.

And Śveta [is white], wearing jeweled earrings, with a crest-lock in front, gentle, and with a serene face; his right hand has a long index finger resembling Śiva, and in his left is a vessel of water. The Buddhist [deity] is Nirvāṇa, a child seated upon a white lotus, always entered into [the heart].
I worship the auspicious Drāviḍa satkavi, the embodiment of the essence of knowledge. (Verse 3) || Contemplation on the Beautiful Form ||
His body is golden, his pair of eyes is adorned with collyrium, his face is bristling with joy, and his hair is tied at the tip of the topknot;
his right hand is joined with a bracelet on its side, his left arm is gracefully extended,
the palms of both hands are curved like flashes of lightning, and he wears earrings upon his ears.
I bow to Sundareśa, who possesses the erotic sentiment, who is a Brahmin of Śiva, who is endowed with all arts,
and whose left side is joined by a golden-hued staff-bearer with a beautiful face, adorned with makara-earrings, and possessing matted locks. (16a, l1–l3)
On the left, she holds the thread of knowledge and the left arm of the Yoginī; in the middle, Śivasundara is in the *tribhaṅga* posture with his feet eternally touching her feet.
This is the meditation on Somāskanda.
Soma-Āskandeśvara is proclaimed [to be located] in the Vāmaka [tradition], while Bhogaśakti is in the southern region; Vīra is seated among the Yogaśaktis,
and Kārttikeya is seated in the center of that, or he is the Vāstu itself.
Four-armed and three-eyed, holding a deer and an axe,
granting fearlessness and adorned with bracelets; his matted hair is decorated with a crescent moon,
with one foot hanging down while the left foot rests upon it.
On the left side, however, is the seated Utpala, endowed with the boon-granting gesture;
the God is accompanied by Umā, adorned in the center by Skanda,
his two hands holding lotus flowers, and he is resplendent in a dancing form.
I worship Somāskandeśvara, who is complete with all auspicious marks.
The Meditation on the Power of Enjoyment:
He has one face, two feet, three eyes, and likewise two arms;
he is joined with two bracelets, assumes the *tribhaṅga* posture, and is adorned with Kerala ornaments.
Adorned with all ornaments and beautified by anklets on the feet—
having fashioned it in this specific manner, it is known as the power of enjoyment (*bhogaśakti*).
The Distinction of Powers.
Having two eyes and two arms, peaceful, red in color, and with two hands;
wrapped in a variegated cloth and adorned with all ornaments;
endowed with full thighs and shanks, and beautified by anklets on the feet.
Having meditated upon the goddess who has a beautiful face, is adorned with celestial ornaments, and is decorated with locks of hair,
and who holds a lotus and a blue water-lily, one should worship her with the mantra. This is the meditation on the youthful Subrahmaṇya.
The Octet of "Protect Me, O Śiva" (Śivapāhi-aṣṭaka)

O Śiva, O Śambhu, protect me—me, a mere mortal, whose intellect is unpeaceful and who wanders through foreign lands across the expanse of the eight directions under the sway of desire; having fashioned me from a mere semblance of a Brahmin, fulfill my purpose!
[I am] submerged in the current of the ocean of the illusion of saṃsāra, bewildered and of unpeaceful intellect.
O Śambhu, protect me—your servant, whose face is brightened by service to your feet, who finds happiness therein, and who is easily overcome by fear; O Śiva, protect me!

O Śambhu, protect me—this vessel of flesh, blood, marrow, impurities, and urine; this body which is a source of pride yet a web of worms and suffering; this one whose limbs are tormented by passion and who is composed of illusion; O Śiva, protect me!

O Śiva, O Śambhu, protect me, who am a mere semblance of a Vedic follower— suddenly ignorant of the Vedas and Āgamas, failing to worship Your lotus feet, and destroying the ritual acts prescribed by the Vedas;
one whose sevenfold mind is intent on acquiring wealth through unjust means, and who is filled with passion for other women.

O Śiva, protect me; O Śambhu, protect me from those who do not eat [the remnants], whose bodies are impure, and who are devoid of right conduct. (5) O Śiva, protect me; O Śambhu, protect me, who am wicked-souled, whose desires are false, who has fallen away from dharma, whose self is ruined, who lacks even a trace of awakening or tranquility, and whose limbs are tormented by the six internal enemies and grievous misfortunes. (6)
Just as a father protects his son, O Lord, so may you, the Father of the Universe, protect me, who am your companion in this world;
O Śiva, O Śambhu, you who are a treasure-house of compassion for all undertakings, protect me even when I have committed an offense.
(7) [O you who are] devoid of means to attain the supreme goal, my body is scorched by the heat of sin and the threefold afflictions. (5)
O Nārāyaṇa, O Śiva, O Śambhu, protect me, a man who has become a non-human in this state of extreme humiliation. 8.
The *Śivapāhy-aṣṭaka* is complete. (pp. 20a–22b). [Full blank page; end of manuscript.]
